title: Notes of Ministry - 90 - May 1980

source.file: Various/Notes of Ministry - 90 - May 1980 (2504)/Notes of Ministry - 90 - May 19 - Various.epub

paragraphs.text: The verse in Ephesians evidently alludes to our physical bodies—“He is Saviour of the body”. It is very comforting to know that, as being in mortal bodies, subject to all that we are subject to in the sufferings and pressures that we experience in our bodies, some more than others, we are thus linked with this great matter of the truth of Christ and the assembly in this emphasis in verse 23 on the Lord being Saviour of the body.

It shows, beloved brethren, how valuable our bodies are to Christ, and His personal interest in our bodies—“He is Saviour of the body”, so that, speaking reverently and humbly, we have a right, you might reverently say, to put in a claim to the Lord in relation to our bodily needs.

When there is sickness or infirmity of body I believe that the Lord would delight to have us remind Him that He is Saviour of the body. The “He”, I think, is very affecting—“He is Saviour of the body”, and, as I have said, I read this physically; it means our actual bodies. It would assume that we have, according to Romans 12, presented our bodies a living sacrifice, which would be acceptable to Him. That He is Saviour of the body, and that that should be linked with this great matter of the mystery, the assembly subjected to Christ, means that we can be confident and free with the Lord about matters to do with our bodies when we need such practical salvation, knowing that “He is Saviour of the body”. That is one of His functions, if we can rightly use

that word; He is that; so we can encourage one another, beloved brethren, as in mortal conditions and weak conditions, that if our outward man is consumed, yet the inward is renewed day by day (2 Corinthians 4: 16). That would be spiritual renewal, while Ephesians 5 alludes to physical salvation.

I wonder if we are sufficiently impressed with the importance of our bodies to the Lord and how He regards them, how He values them, and how He is prepared to serve us in such detail in relation to them in every test; and as long as we are here we shall always have these tests.

There are many among us who are now going through testing conditions. We think of a beloved sister, for instance, and what she has endured today in that regard, and others who are with us too who are going through these actual trials. What a comfort this verse is to us, and the fact that “He” is italicised—“He is Saviour of the body”; so we can count on that as long as we are down here, as long as we are in the body, that He is Saviour of the body. He has that direct interest, and that direct service which He carries on, and yet it would involve our drawing, you might say, on what is available to us in relation to our bodies. How often we forget, and, perhaps, we go to the doctor—which is right enough because he is part of God’s angelic provision—but the great thing to keep in mind in all these testings—and they are testings—is that He is Saviour of the body.
In Philippians we are given this wonderful fact that He is going to change our bodies of humiliation. It is not ‘vile bodies’, as in the Authorised Version, but “body of humiliation”.

We feel it more as we get older that our bodies are bodies of humiliation. It is no disgrace to feel that. It is because we are mortal, but relates to what happened at the fall; so mortality is evident in us;

and yet He is going to change all that in a moment, and not only remove the effects of the humiliation but change our bodies to be like His own body of glory. What a thing that is to think about! I remember a brother when very sick and suffering saying, ‘Well, I am a prisoner to my body; I cannot do anything; I cannot get away from the pain, or the weakness’. But what a comfort that He is going to relieve us of all that and transform these very bodies. He is going to transform these bodies of humiliation to be like His own body of glory. I think that verse of Mr. Darby’s—if you can make comparisons—is like the top note.
‘Like Jesus! Grace supreme!
Like Him ...’ (Hymn 72)
That will be actually so in our bodies; we shall have bodies like unto His body of glory.

Then just a word about the solemn side in Corinthians, which brings in our responsibility. It is very solemn that Paul, one so committed and spiritual, should have this concern as to responsibility for keeping his body right. That is not now a question of physical fitness; it is a question of moral fitness, keeping right morally through constant self-judgment. That is what this buffeting the body would be. We would be sober about the value of our bodies to Christ in the testimony. We need a body to be in the testimony. We cannot be in the testimony effectively without a body, and we cannot be in the testimony effectively if we are careless about our bodies. I do not mean careless physically, I mean careless morally. Perhaps we are not buffeting them as Paul did. This is a very real matter, that we are to be severe on ourselves about anything we are conscious is a hindrance to us. That would apply to everyone, even the youngest. We must learn to deny ourselves, and the power to be used is the Spirit; “If, by the Spirit, ye put to death the deeds of the
body, ye shall live”, Romans 8: 13. It is a question of being maintained in usability to the Lord in the testimony, and not being rejected.

What a wonderful thing it is that the Lord should deign to use us, which requires our bodies, but then we need to be on the qui vive, we need to be on the alert all the time, lest the enemy should be getting any advantage through any carelessness on our part, through not habitually buffeting our bodies, as Paul says, because of the possibility of our being rejected. It is a severe thing and it is Paul who says it; but he did it. He buffeted his body, which would be characteristic. He learned to deny himself, and we must learn to do that if we are going to be constantly serviceable; whatever we have been in the past we should be no less in the future; but it depends not only on His being Saviour of the body physically, but our answering to our responsibility in dealing severely with ourselves in anything that would hinder us from being serviceable to the Lord in the testimony.

What a privilege it is, beloved brethren, that in this broken day He should take us up in conditions of mortality and weakness, knowing all that marks us, and yet saying that this is possible, and, indeed, you might say, that this is normal. That is what Paul would say, ‘It is normal; I do this habitually’. It is like your daily exercises. The doctor may say, ‘You should take certain exercises every day for your health’; and that is what Paul was doing; he was taking regular moral exercise to keep himself in trim and to keep the enemy out, for the enemy would damage us. So let us, beloved brethren, use care over our bodies, you might say spiritually, so that we might not become less usable. We might even become unusable. That is not what the Lord desires. There is the responsible side, and it is not pleasant; but the only way to be kept in power is by this rule that Paul practised in a characteristic way by buffeting his body and keeping it under lest he should be rejected.
Scripture tells us that God is “preserver of all men, specially of those that believe”, 1 Timothy 4: 10. The circumstances surrounding our brother’s death were both unusual and sorrowful.

Let us not, however, feel that God’s protecting hand was not over our brother. In God’s wisdom He allowed the circumstances which led to his death. The passage read from Matthew’s gospel shows how Satan will even use Scripture to lead us to tempt God as to His care for us. The Lord would not allow Himself to take any action that would put Himself in the position of testing out the reality of God’s care of Him. I feel that this is a word to us, dear brethren. Our circumstances should not be such as to tempt God in His care of us, particularly if we are living alone, as our brother was. We know that our brother was concerned about living nearer to the meeting room, where he would be in closer contact with the brethren, but that desire was never realised. I do not dwell further on that side of things save to say that it is not sufficient for us just to say that we have faith that God will care for us. God would expect us to see that our surroundings and circumstances are such that His care for us is not tempted.

The passage in Deuteronomy relates to the way that God leads us for our spiritual education and blessing. Jacob, shortly before he died, could speak of the “God that shepherded me all my life long”, Genesis 48: 15. Our brother has had a long life; it was over sixty years ago that I first met him. He then was interested in the truth to the extent that he attended the meetings frequently and also purchased a complete set of J. N. Darby’s ‘Collected Writings’ and F. E.

Raven’s ‘Lectures’, both of which may have provided a fund of spiritual instruction for him during his lifetime. We know little about many years of that time prior to his relatively recent years when he was able to realise what had been in his heart ever since those early days—to enjoy, with the brethren, the ministry of the truth in a sphere of salvation and peace. The interim, under God’s hand, undoubtedly was used for some formation, but it was God’s intent that he should be blessed in his latter end. His “latter end”, as I refer to it, is the part of his life that is known to most of us with whom he has walked in fellowship these recent years.

We know the comfort that he has found, and the joy that his presence amongst us has been to us all, but specially to his local brethren. We know what a bright, lovable believer he was, and we appreciated the way in which he demonstrated in his manner of life the practical character of divine teaching. All this, I suggest, would be related to God ‘doing him good’ in his “latter end”.

The Epistle to the Hebrews speaks of God’s disciplinary ways with us, of the way in which as a father God chastens His sons, causing us to go through various experiences so that our sinful nature may be thoroughly judged and full room made for the liberty and activity of the Holy Spirit in us. This is the latter end reached, as that epistle says—“afterwards yields the peaceful fruit

of righteousness to those exercised by it”, Hebrews 12: 11. Our dear brother has had this experience; he reached the ‘afterwards’ amongst his brethren. It has been a great joy to witness his development in the truth, the appreciation he had of a fellowship which, through most of his life, he had desired to have part in. God blessed him in his latter end, for which we give thanks.

The death of our brother has reminded us that sometimes the Lord moves suddenly from His own side. The Lord has a right to do this in our lives. He moved that way in relation to Paul of whom we have read. At the time of Saul’s conversion it says that “suddenly there shone round about him a light out of heaven”, and the Lord’s voice brought about the conversion of Saul of Tarsus, who was later called Paul. So it was very sudden with Paul, and I referred to this section to show how the Lord came in suddenly to intervene in the circumstances in which these two ministers found themselves, and then how matters opened up for the blessing of the gaoler. How wonderful that the Lord in grace moves according to His own skill and wisdom to reach out and to bring in blessing!

Our brother moved in and out amongst us as a man with a beautiful spirit, the spirit of Jesus. I believe all of us would recognise that the most effective thing that we can have is the spirit of that Man who is seated at the right hand of God, and this is what our brother set out. Every one

of us, I think, would know what it has been to have our affections drawn out to our dear brother who is now with Christ. It is a wonderful thing, a great comfort to all of us, that Paul speaks of “departure and being with Christ” which is “very much better”, Philippians 1: 23.
So we can think of our brother, full of years, but now his part with Christ is very much better.

It is interesting to see the way the Lord moved in his circumstances so that things happened very quickly. It was only a couple of weeks ago that our brother was in our home, and he said to me at that time, ‘If the Lord should take me, I am ready to go’. I just wonder whether all of us could say that, whether we, each one of us, in our own links with the Lord Jesus, would be able to say, ‘If the Lord takes me, I am ready to go’.

Here Paul and Silas were in prison. They were coming into Europe to preach the glad tidings, and we know that there is a tremendous power against the glad tidings; the enemy is against the idea of the word getting into my heart and into your heart. These men had come to preach; they had come to spread the glad tidings, to bring within the range of men the glory of what God’s thoughts are for them. God “desires that all men should be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth”, 1 Timothy 2: 4. Well, the enemy had them put in gaol, but at midnight, the most difficult moment, you might say, in the middle of the night, they were singing. What a victory over their circumstances! And the prisoners heard them.

Then it says, “suddenly”; I read this because of the force of how the Lord comes into a situation suddenly, as He did in the life of our brother. He came in suddenly at various times, and even in his departure He came in suddenly; but our brother

was ready. Well, He came in suddenly here with an earthquake; and this earthquake reached right into the soul of the gaoler, who would have committed suicide. He would have taken his own life for fear that the prisoners that he was supposed to guard had fled. But Paul says, “Do thyself no harm, for we are all here”. And then the gaoler comes in and says to Paul and Silas,
“Sirs, what must I do that I may be saved?”

Well, it is like our brother in his own life, how he worked things out in his own relations with the Lord Jesus, so that he could say, ‘I am ready if the Lord should take me”. And why was he ready? Because he had come to know the Lord Jesus Christ as his own personal Saviour.

That is what set him up so that he was ready. Paul and Silas say to the gaoler, “Believe on the Lord Jesus and thou shalt be saved, thou and thy house”. Oh, what a message! Some of us here are householders, and we want to be sure our households are saved.

Our brother basked in the joy of his salvation; he basked in the joy of his knowledge of Christ as his own personal Saviour. The conditions are the same, coming right down to the day in which we are, gathered here to bury our brother, who was in the joy of these things. We can say that the word to us now, coming in suddenly under these circumstances, is the same,
“Believe on the Lord Jesus and thou shalt be saved, thou and thy house”.

What a glorious object of faith Christ is! And He is available to us as our hearts would be softened at a time such as this; it is a time when we are softened, a time when we are amenable, a time when the word of God can have entrance into our hearts. May we know what it is to receive into our affections, and have as an object of faith, our Lord Jesus who has accomplished everything for
God and everything for men. May we embrace Him and know what it is to have salvation—“thou and thy house”. May it be so.

articles.title: DIVINE SYMPATHIES
articles.author: T. E. Druckenmiller
articles.meeting: Words at the burial of Mr, R. C. McDowell

paragraphs.text: The thought of the sympathies of divine Persons for us has come into one’s heart, beloved brethren and friends. Our households are a sphere where divine affections are to be known.

The enemy’s power is set against our households; he is set against the preciousness of a family, against the very thought of a family. But I believe the Lord Jesus would impress our hearts afresh at this time with the value of our families, and increase in our affections the value of the family of God, what it is to be here for the Lord Jesus Christ in the simplicity set out in the life of our beloved brother. The value of what has been expressed in the life of our brother is, I believe, to be expressed in every one of our lives. The Father has given His own Son, the Lord Jesus Christ, and it is the coming into manhood of Jesus that has expressed in this scene among men the very impress of divine feelings.

So in John 11, where death had come in—and it is in the presence of death that God has a way of speaking to our hearts peculiarly—that it says that “Jesus wept”. Then it says, “The Jews therefore said, Behold how he loved him!” Think of the love of Jesus for this one who had departed. It says earlier in the chapter that “Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus”. The love of Jesus is for us all, it is toward us, the love of God expressed in that glorious Man who came into manhood and who went into death itself; but in His movements among men divine sympathies were expressed. In every contact He had with man in his need, whether it be Lazarus, who had died, or the woman in John 4 in all her need, or you or me in all our need, divine love is toward us today, just as it has always been. May we just allow our hearts to open to it.

Then, as to Luke 15, it has touched one’s heart to think of the way our brother enjoyed the Father’s love. This chapter peculiarly sets out the feelings of divine Persons. You get the thought of a sheep being lost, and one going a long way to find it. You get the thought of a piece of silver being lost, and the diligence of love to seek carefully till she found it, and then, what we know all of us so well, the prodigal son gone away into a far country. How the father felt it! We get in the end of the Old Testament, in the last verse of that precious portion of God’s word, “He shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers”; that is what God is doing currently. The enemy is working the other way, to bring in disunity in the family, but God from His side is working to bring in right feelings and affections in our hearts, stirring them with a view to our expressing divine sympathies as we walk here.

Our beloved brother expressed that—divine sympathies. One recalls how he could refer to this verse, where it expresses the father’s feelings—“Bring out the best robe and clothe him in it, and put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet”. That is what the Father wants to do with every one of us, to clothe us, to bring us into the liberty and the merriment of His own sphere.

Well, may we be drawn into it today, as it says, “they began to make merry”. Oh, let us be in that merriment, in the rejoicing and the liberty and fulness of sonship. How our brother enjoyed it! and we are stirred with affection for those who were near to him in his own family. How he loved them! May we be encouraged and stimulated in our affections to yield our hearts to the Lord Jesus Christ, to come into the enjoyment of divine sympathies, and thus to express the love of Christ in our lives, one toward another, in view of family affection being known and enjoyed among us, for His name’s sake.
P.

The tent of meeting was a very remarkable structure, and everything that was made, to form part of it, has its application for us. I have been thinking of the curtains and the veil about which we have read. The area of the tabernacle consisted of three parts, and each had an entrance which was hung with a curtain or veil. Perhaps we could consider these entrances a little more closely. They are given to us in the following order according to the thoughts of God: the first led into the holiest of all; the next into the holy place, and the third into the court of the tabernacle. So far as our experience is concerned the order is reversed and the court comes first. Anyone who saw the tabernacle and wished to go in came first to the entrance that led into the court.

Both the curtains, and the veil, were made from the same material, and the four different colours in them represent Christ to us. The Lord Himself made it clear that no one comes to the Father unless by Him. Whoever wished to go into the court, the holy place, or the holiest, must go in through the curtains, or the veil—that is, through Christ; and our enjoyment of this blessed sphere can only be through Him. All who are here today have already entered into the court, as has everyone who has received the forgiveness of sins through the grace of Christ.

In the court was the brazen altar. Brass speaks of the judgment of sin, something that we must learn, the judgment that Christ bore. The first entrance—into the court—was wider than the others and that means that there is enough room for everyone— all are invited. So the court presents to us the great foundational truths of christianity.
But God does not wish to have us just on the border of His world. The assembly is the first of all the families in heaven or on earth, it is the assembly of the firstborn (Hebrews 12: 23).

God would have us in more intimate nearness, not merely in the court, therefore even greater things have been prepared for us. We have seen that brass speaks of judgment, but in the holy place everything was of gold. God desires us to be where everything corresponds with Himself, and that involves the assembly. The second curtain refers to the fact that only through Christ can we go in to the holy place, an area which involves that the Holy Spirit brings about conformity to Christ in us. The furniture in the holy place represents the saints as set together and looking into the wonderful word of God. The lampstand and the table of shewbread were there, that is, there is light and food for the saints. Where do we find that?—in the assembly as we consider Christ and enquire into the Scriptures that speak of Himself.

But God desires still more for us. He wishes that we should be in nearness to Himself, in the holiest of all. Through Christ’s death the veil was rent, that is, God has come out and is revealed to us. The curtain was rent because God came out. As to our side, we have been invited in, for we find in Hebrews no mention of the veil as rent. We find there the priestly service of our Lord, so that we can through Him enter into the very presence of God “by the blood of Jesus, the new and living way which he has dedicated for us through the veil, that is, his flesh”, Hebrews 10: 19, 20. Thus we enter the holiest of all.

Perhaps we could compare John 14: 6 with the three entrances. Jesus said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life”. Whoever desires to enter must find the way, that is Christ—answering to the court. Entering the holy place we find light and food, that is the truth, and entering the holiest of all, through the veil, we find Christ, the life; we enjoy life there. Thus we can see that Christ has become everything to us. These types should preserve us from standing still, for it is God’s will that we should have life abundantly. A place has been prepared for us in His very presence. When He gives it is not in part but in fulness, in abundance; it is the best; nearness to Himself, His own presence, there to have part in His joy. May we enjoy it more and more, and as this is so the love of God abides in us.

I have been impressed since Lord’s day as to the need to take on change and features of glory. If this is God’s mind for us, and assuredly it is, He has an object before Him—that we should arrive at conformity to the Lord Jesus. It is not only that certain features of the Lord Jesus should come to light in us, but we should have before us God’s complete thought. It has rightly been said that Christ is God’s ideal. He is there in the presence of God and God rests complacently in Him. His mind being that the saints should be conformed to that blessed Man. How often we compare ourselves with others; and we, are so accustomed to imperfect thoughts, substitutes, and synthetics; but God has in mind perfection, and that is seen in the Lord Jesus. It will take every believer to set out all the features that are seen in the Lord Jesus. The new man involves every believer.

How low the Lord Jesus has been that the will of God might be done. Typically, in Jonah 2: 5, it is said that He has been to the bottoms of the mountains, and the weeds were wrapped about His head. He is the One who descended; how our minds should be affected by that!

“He that descended is the same who has also ascended up above all the heavens”. Oh what a height He has gone to; He has “passed through the heavens”, Hebrews 4: 14. Mr. Taylor said that every sphere was filled with Him as He passed through (see N.S. Vol.1 p.20)—that triumphant Man, and He is there above all the heavens that He might
fill all things.

From that position He has given gifts in view of the inauguration of christianity, the setting up of the assembly here. While some gifts do not continue to the present time, what is authoritative does continue. We do not have apostles, but authority continues. God would have it that there is authority in the assembly at the present time, and that it should be respected, that what is said in ministry under the headship of Christ, and in the power of the Holy Spirit, should be listened to.

So gift continues in view of the saints arriving at God’s ideal. It has been said that the gifts are like a scaffolding; they surround the building and you may not altogether see what is proceeding inside, but there is construction going on, the gifts are operating, and what is going into the building is substantial. God is proceeding with His building; we may not see much in small numbers here and there, but what is coming out of it all is formation, and conformity to God’s ideal, the Lord Jesus Christ.

He has in mind that we should arrive at that, “until we all arrive”—until we all arrive. We had on Lord’s day, “We all, looking on the glory of the Lord, with unveiled face, are transformed according to the same image” (2 Corinthians 3: 18), and here it is, “until we all arrive ... at the full-grown man, at the measure of the stature of the fulness of the Christ”—

that is God’s ideal for every believer. Eventually there will be no need for gift. The gifts will have served their purpose and the work will be complete. What God has before Him is a great and august vessel composed of persons conformed to the image of His Son. God is working to a certain end. How aimless we tend to be, but God has a purpose in mind in all that He

does. We may not see it, it may be obscure to us, but He is working according to His own thoughts, and He will secure them and have the saints conformed to His ideal. We sometimes sing of ‘the perfect state’ [hymn 247); what it will be, beloved brethren, when every one will be conformed to Christ!

In Philippians 3 Paul is stretching out to the things before. It is not the exercise of gift here; the beloved apostle in his own personal exercises is setting out something that should mark each one of us, and that is energy in view of arriving at Christ where He is. You see the energy, the stretching out, the zeal, that marked Paul to arrive at his object. He was not just stationary in his exercises, he pursued, “forgetting the things behind, and stretching out to the things before ... for the prize of the calling on high of God in Christ Jesus”. What an object he had before him; Christ filled his heart. How lurch he could have laid claim to; how much he could have used to make much of himself; but he counted all things to be loss on account of the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus his Lord. So we see Paul, with Christ in glory before him, stretching out with zeal. Well, beloved brethren, is this our object? Have we that aim energetically before us, to reach out to Christ where He is, in view of conformity to Him?

Epaphras was a local brother in Colosse, not an outstandingly gifted man, as far as we can gather from the Scriptures, but one who had genuine concern for his local brethren; and he had an ideal before him. His desire was that the saints should stand perfect and complete in all the will of God. That would involve devotion in the testimony here and holding on to God’s thoughts, so that things are maintained inviolate, not having

our own thoughts, not lowering the standard, but that the saints should arrive at standing perfect and complete in all the will of God. Well, we know that there are such men, persons in their own local settings who have an ideal for the saints. Oh that we might have that, an ideal for one another, so that we might pray accordingly. I feel challenged as to this. How little we pray in relation to formation in the saints, in relation to the saints arriving at what God has in mind for them. We pray for the circumstantial needs of the saints, and how right that we should; but we should desire that the saints might stand perfect and complete in all the will of God. Epaphras had an ideal for the saints in Colosse. May that be our ideal.

I refer to Stephen because we see in him the features of Christ coming out in an individual believer in outstanding quality. How near to his Master he came; how close to the Lord Jesus in his suffering, and in his feelings expressed as he died, his desire, “Lord, lay not this sin to their charge”. I feel the challenge of it. How near do we come to the Lord Jesus as He pursued His suffering pathway here? Stephen was very close to Christ in His sufferings; he was “a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit”, Acts 6: 5. You think of the substantiality that was there, the formation in him, and it is seen in his death. When the saints are in circumstances of suffering it brings out what is there in genuineness and quality, the work of God. You can see it in believers who suffer in their bodies; what comes to light is the perfection of the work of God.

So Stephen here is suffering; men are throwing stones at him, but he is not thinking of that; he has his eye on Christ in glory. “He saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing ...”. What a sight!—looking right into heaven, seeing that Man in glory.

and representing Him here in testimony. What perfection came out in Stephen; how near to his Master he came—occupied with Him there, and coming out like Him here. We can see how Stephen was formed. As quite a young man, I suppose, he had served at tables. His service did not go on for long—how short it was—but at the end of it he went out in triumph, like his Master.

O, beloved brethren, may this be our portion that, having Christ before us, looking upon Him, and being transformed from glory to glory, there may be greater conformity to Christ in view of that day when we shall be presented to Him, and that now, in testimony, greater formation may mark us as features of Christ come to light in us. May it be so, for His name’s sake.
He came! He came! A Babe laid in a manger;
Grew up; a Child, a Boy, a Man indeed;
Down here in grace a lowly heavenly Stranger,
Delighting God and meeting every need.
Jesus my Saviour, Jesus my Friend,
Proving Thy grace, Lord, on Thee I do depend.
He died! He died!—O what a sad reflection
That wicked men have crucified God’s Son!
To God a sacrifice in full perfection,
For men sins borne, a place in glory won,
Jesus my Saviour, Jesus my Friend,
Deep were the depths, Lord, to which Thou didst descend.
He lives! He lives! A blessed Man in glory,
Raised from the dead by God’s almighty power,
Seated on high, O what a wondrous story
Of love for sinners, proved in death’s dark hour.
Jesus my Saviour. Jesus my Friend,
Living to Thee, Lord, my praises will ascend.
He comes! He comes! What joyful expectation!
The Lord will rapture all His own away,
The church’s hope then brought to realisation,
As with His saints He comes forth in display.
Jesus my Saviour, Jesus my Friend,
I may hear today, Lord, that call to ascend.
London, 1979

articles.title: “TEACH US TO NUMBER OUR DAYS”
articles.author: F. C. Mutton
articles.meeting: Substance of word in meeting for ministry

paragraphs.text: We were reminded on Lord’s day of the divine ‘dip into time’, and of what God has wrought, and is still working out, in time in view of eternity, according to His eternal purpose. This psalm speaks of God being “from eternity to eternity”; it also speaks of various periods of time— “a thousand years”, then “threescore years and ten” and “four-score years”; then it refers to our days. As we think of the brevity of life compared with eternity it should impress upon us the value of each day.

This is a psalm of Moses, the man of God, the product of his rich experience with God. What an experience that was—forty years in the court of Pharaoh and then forty years looking after someone else’s sheep. How would any of us like forty years

keeping sheep in a wilderness? But all through that history Moses was learning God and being formed in view of the great responsibility he was to have during his forty years with Israel in the wilderness. Through it he became a man of God.

All this bears upon us, especially as we are feeling the death of our beloved sister in Edinburgh. We think of the brevity of the life of Jesus here and of all that was concentrated in it. All that shall be displayed millennially and pass into eternity is the fruit of that life, and of His death. Then there is what God is working out in our lives. How tiny they are compared with eternity; yet how much God would secure in them in view of eternity.

This morning I walked by Bo’ness Academy and I thought, ‘This is one more essential day in the education of those hundreds of young people, another day in their few years of education to fit them for life’. We are in the school of God for the brief period of our lives, to form us for the day of display, and for eternity. So Moses says, “Teach us to number our days”. Let us value each day. Let us be with God as we start each one, and as we go through each one, so that there is something for Him out of it. Let our circumstances day by day yield something as we go through them with Him. Most of our lives are fairly ordinary, as the poet said,
‘The common round, the daily task.
Will furnish all we ought to ask’.

So as we meet the little tests, problems, maybe disappointments and sorrows of each day, let us go through them with God, so that as we learn our lessons in His school the flesh may be worn down and what is according to Christ built up.
So Moses says, “Let the beauty of Jehovah our

God be upon us”—that would be like Paul’s word in 2 Corinthians 6: 11, “that the life also of Jesus may be manifested in our mortal flesh”. Thus each day in the lives of the saints, amid the ordinary circumstances in which we move, the great divine work is to proceed, the result of which shall be displayed is its magnificent aggregate of glory in the world to come, and subsist for divine pleasure eternally.
Let us then learn to number our days, and be with God in each of them, so that none of them may be wasted, but each yield something in formation after Christ.

We have to walk about refusing the things that invite us, learning always to refer to the Spirit of God, proving that you have no friend in this world but the Spirit. If you live in the Spirit, walk in the Spirit ... the christian has everything against him in this world, his only help is from the Spirit of God, and if he does not walk in the Spirit he is worse off than a good moral man of the world. You have to refer to the Spirit of God for everything, the moment you want any other help you are in danger.

Just think of it for a moment! Suppose you and I are the objects of the Father’s love, what could go wrong with us? Is it not a scene of perfect serenity? What could be wrong there? To think that He loves me! He has quickened me because He
loves me! That is the secret! What I am in the presence of the Father is not for my satisfaction but for His.

This proposal on the Lord’s part to rest is very touching—“Come ye yourselves apart ... and rest a little”. Some of us have been calculating the time spent by Israel in sabbath according to the types—it would average, in fifty years, thirty-eight per cent of their time. The Lord, I think, would remind us that for effective ministry there should be sabbath-keeping.

The more you apprehend “Jesus Christ” and then ‘God’s Son’ (Galatians 1), the more will be your abhorrence of yourself, and to this end I believe God would direct us in our histories to see what one has been. It is not just flesh, but it is the flesh in me. Paul was speaking of what was in himself. It is a very wholesome consideration and helps us all the more to appreciate the grace that has delivered us, not only from the world, but from ourselves, and made us superior to all that now.

The secret of the want of guidance with many of God’s people is just this, that selfishness is at the bottom of their exercises; whereas a righteous holy calculation in a time of uncertainty will certainly bring us into light.
